Polynomial mixing for stochastic viscous conservation law equation on the whole line

Peng Gao ††thanks: School of Mathematics and Statistics, Center for Mathematics and Interdisciplinary Sciences, Northeast Normal University, Changchun, China. Email: gaopengjilindaxue@126.com    Liying Li ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen, China. Email: lily@sustech.edu
Abstract

In this paper, we study the long-time behavior of the viscous conservation law equation on the whole real line, subject to a white-in-time force and arbitrarily small damping and viscosity constants. We establish polynomial mixing rates in two settings: (a) a general super-quadratic flux with hyperviscous dissipation, where the growth of the nonlinearity is controlled by the order of hyperviscosity, and the force is sufficiently non-degenerate on a generic L2L^{2}-basis; and (b) a general quadratic flux with standard second-order dissipation, and the force is non-degenerate on some unconditional basis. Both settings include the classical Burgers-type nonlinearity. The proof is based on an abstract polynomial coupling criterion developed in [Gao26] and a Foiaş–Prodi estimate.

MSC 2020: 37A25, 37A30, 60H15

Keywords: polynomial mixing; viscous conservation law equation; viscous Burgers equation; Foiaş–Prodi estimate; coupling method

1 Introduction

The viscous conservation law equation is an important class of partial differential equations (PDEs). It provides a fundamental and complete description of real compressible flows across all speed regimes. In this paper, we consider the (damped) viscous conservation law equation with random forcing in one dimension

ut+au+ν(−∂x​x)γ/2u+(F(u))x=fω,ν,γ>0,a≥0.u_{t}+au+\nu(-\partial_{xx})^{\gamma/2}u+\bigl(F(u)\bigr)_{x}=f^{\omega},\quad\nu,\gamma>0,\ a\geq 0. (1.1)

Equation 1.1 captures two competing physical mechanisms: nonlinear convection that steepens flow gradients into shock waves or shear layers, and viscous dissipation that smooths these sharp discontinuities through internal friction and thermal conduction. When the flux F=u2/2F=u^{2}/2 is quadratic, equation 1.1 reduces to the Burgers equation, which was introduced initially [Bur40, Bur74] as a simplified fluid equation to study the turbulence. The addition of a (small) dissipative term is motivated by the vanishing-viscosity selection principle, which states that the physically relevant solutions of the inviscid conservation law can be recovered by the solutions of the viscous equation in the ν→0\nu\to 0 limit. The selection principle is expected to hold not only for the usual second derivative, but also for general dissipative term. Rigorous results have been established for fractional dissipation γ∈(0,2]\gamma\in(0,2] [Dro03, Ali07], while higher-order and fractional dissipations γ≥2\gamma\geq 2 extend this mechanism and arise naturally in the study of hyperviscous conservation laws and turbulence [Tad04, Ban19].

The primary goal of this paper is to understand the long-time behavior of 1.1, particularly the existence and uniqueness of stationary states and the rate of mixing. The study of this topic has several motivations. From a physical viewpoint, this is a natural model for non-equilibrium statistical dynamics, as the energy injected into the system by the force is balanced by the dissipation effect. With quadratic flux, the stochastic Burgers equation shares similar nonlinearity to the Navier–Stokes nonlinearity, and is one of the simplest models in which aspects of turbulence can be studied rigorously [BK21, Kuk24]. The stochastic PDE (SPDE) can also be viewed as an infinite-dimensional random dynamical system or Markov process, and it is interesting to see how dissipation, nonlinear transport, and stochastic forcing interact to determine its ergodic properties.

For the mixing property of 1.1 on the real line that is studied in this paper, we have to add a non-zero damping a>0a>0 to control the low-frequency mode; this is a unavoidable technical assumption since our coupling techniques depends on partial differential equation energy estimates. For similar problems on bounded domains, such damping effect is already provided by the boundedness of the domain itself, so one can take a=0a=0. If merely the existence and uniqueness of stationary solutions are concerned, then certain probabilistic methods can bypass the damping addition, as we will see below. For the long-term behavior of randomly forced viscous conservation laws, there are only a few results available. The invariant measure for such equations was studied in [DV15, CP19, DDG+23] and the references therein. Compared with the above works, a notable feature of our contribution is that we are able to establish polynomial mixing on the whole line, a setting not covered in previous studies.

The ergodic proprieties of 1.1 and related equations have been extensively studied in the past thirty years. On 𝕋d\mathbb{T}^{d}, the results are usually stated for the stochastic Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation

∂th+F⁡(∇h)=ν​Δ​h+f~ω.\partial_{t}h+F(\nabla h)=\nu\Delta h+\tilde{f}^{\omega}. (1.2)

In dimension one, 1.2 is the integrated form of 1.1 with a=0a=0 and γ=2\gamma=2, namely, if hh solves 1.2, then u=∂xhu=\partial_{x}h solves 1.1 with f=f~f=\tilde{f}. The flux function FF is the Hamiltonian in the HJB equation. In higher dimensions the resulting equation from u=∇hu=\nabla h only generalizes 1.1 if additionally uu and fωf^{\omega} are gradient fields. In this setup, it has been proven that, under fairly general assumptions of the random forcing, in every dimension, for all convex Hamiltonians, for both positive viscosity and zero-viscosity, there is a unique stationary solution uu for every prescribed average velocity v=∫𝕋du∈ℝdv=\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}u\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, a One Force — One Solution principle holds, and the dynamics is exponentially mixing [Sin91, EKMS00, IK03, DS05, GIKP05, BK13, DV15, KZ17, Bor18, IKZ20]; moreover, the viscous stationary solutions will converge to the inviscid ones in the ν→0\nu\to 0 limit [EKMS00, GIKP05].

On the whole space ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, the ergodic problems of 1.1 is much harder, as the compactness is lost in many aspects: the domains, the functional spaces, the embedding structures and so on. There are two kinds of forcing to consider: the first kind of forcing is to take fω​(t,x)f^{\omega}(t,x) as a spatially homogeneous random processes in xx, which is a direct generalization of the periodic setting; the second kind is to allow fω​(t,x)f^{\omega}(t,x) to have suitable decays as |x|→∞\lvert x\rvert\to\infty, so the noise will provide certain compactification effects.

For undamped Burgers equation with homogeneous force on ℝ\mathbb{R}, there is an analogous picture to the periodic case: for every prescribed properly defined “average velocity” vv, there exists a unique stationary solutions. This was first established for inviscid Burgers in [BCK14, Bak16], and then in the viscous case in [BL19]. The inviscid limit of the stationary solutions is proven in [BL18]. The exact quadratic form of FF of the Burgers equation allows reformulation of the ergodic problems in terms of infinite geodesics or infinite-volume polymer measures, and various probabilistic estimates then apply. Similar results are also established in [DGR21] using more a PDE-based approach. Later [DDG+23] shows existence of stationary solutions for at least some sparse set of velocity. It is worth noting that in all these results, the uniqueness part comes purely from the comparison principle and the ordering of one-dimensional space, and thus cannot be extended to higher dimensions. Another motivation to study the one-dimensional HJB equation with fast-decorrelated homogeneous force is that it is conjectured to belong to the Kardar–Parisi–Zhang (KPZ) universality class. This has been proven rigorously for many integrable models like the KPZ equation itself, i.e., 1.2 with quadratic FF and f~\tilde{f} the space-time white noise [ACQ11, MQR21], while for general stochastic conservation laws it is wide open; we refer to [BK18] for more discussion in this direction.

For the undamped stochastic Burgers equation with decaying force, using probabilistic representation of the solutions, existence and uniqueness of stationary solutions are also established in some settings [HK03, BK10, Bak13]. A exponential mixing rate is only established in [BK10] where the forcing creates a deep trap near the origin. The goal of this paper is to establish mixing rate of 1.1 with more general L2L^{2}-noises, following the coupling approach developed in [Shi08, KS12, Gao26].

Mixing rates of SPDEs on the whole space is generally difficult from the viewpoint of PDEs. Even with a positive damping, one still does not have Poincaré inequality or compact Sobolev embedding which are essential for the parallel programs in bounded domains. Recently, [NZ24a] establishes exponential mixing for the complex Ginzburg–Landau equation on the real line by combining weighted Foiaş–Prodi estimates with the classical coupling method, which provides a powerful methodological framework. The work [Gao26] shows polynomial mixing of 1.1 with γ=4\gamma=4, by extending the coupling method and establishing an abstract criterion for polynomial mixing of Markov processes. Here, the order of polynomial mixing is arbitrarily high, but the constant before the decay rate will depend on the order. This framework is later applied to obtain polynomial mixing for the white-forced Navier-Stokes system in the whole space [NZ24b] and the white-forced wave equation on the whole line [Gao24]. In all these results, the random force is assumed to take the form

fω​(t,x)=h+η,η=∂∂t​(∑j=1∞bj​ej​(x)​βj​(t)),f^{\omega}(t,x)=h+\eta,\quad\eta=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}b_{j}e_{j}(x)\beta_{j}(t)), (1.3)

where {ej​(x)}j=1∞\{e_{j}(x)\}_{j=1}^{\infty} is an orthonormal basis in H=L2​(ℝ)H=L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) or H1​(ℝ)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}), {βj​(t)}j=1∞\{\beta_{j}(t)\}_{j=1}^{\infty} is a family of independent Wiener process, and hh is a fixed element in HH satisfying some controllability condition. The only non-degeneracy condition imposed is that bj≠0b_{j}\neq 0 for 1≤j≤N1\leq j\leq N, where NN depends on the basis and the number a,ν>0a,\nu>0.

This paper extends and continues the line of research initiated in [Gao26]. Our original motivation is to develop a weighted Foiaş–Prodi estimate for the classical Burgers equation where γ=2\gamma=2. However, the nonlinearity of the Burgers equation and general conservation law is worse than that of the Navier–Stokes equation, in the sense that there is no cancellation of convection term in the absence of divergence-free condition ∇⋅u=0\nabla\cdot u=0. We handle the nonlinearity in two approaches. The first approach is to use extra regularity provided by superviscosity γ>2\gamma>2. This generalizes [Gao26] where γ=4\gamma=4, and also allows the flux function to grow super-quadratically where the growth exponent is controlled by γ\gamma; see H2. The second approach is to keep the usual second order dissipation, but assume additionally that the L2L^{2}-basis {ej}j=1∞\{e_{j}\}_{j=1}^{\infty} appearing in 1.3 also forms an unconditional basis in HsH^{s} for some s>0s>0; see H3. We then use a new Poincaré inequality (see Lemma 4.2) to obtain a Foiaş–Prodi estimate that can treat all flux functions with a most quadratic growth.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we present the precise assumptions and main results of this paper. In Section 3, we first recall the well-posedness theory of 1.1 via the variational framework, and then present the abstract criterion for polynomial mixing of Markov processes in [Gao26] and sketch the construction of the coupling extension. In Section 4, we derive weighted Foiaş–Prodi estimates for 1.1, which are the key step in verifying the abstract criterion. In Section 5 we establish several energy estimates and stopping time properties that will be used in the proof of the main theorem, which will be done in Section 6. In the appendix, we collect some functional inequalities and auxiliary estimates that will be used in this paper.

2 Main result

We consider the stochastic viscous conservation law

ut+au+ν(−∂x​x)1+κu+(F(u))x=h+η,u(t,x):ℝ2→ℝ,u_{t}+au+\nu(-\partial_{xx})^{1+\kappa}u+\bigl(F(u)\bigr)_{x}=h+\eta,\quad u(t,x):\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R}, (2.1)

where ν,a>0,κ≥0\nu,a>0,\ \kappa\geq 0, η\eta is given by 1.3, {ej​(x)}j=1∞\{e_{j}(x)\}_{j=1}^{\infty} is an orthonormal basis in H:=L2​(ℝ)H:=L^{2}(\mathbb{R}), and {βj​(t)}j=1∞\{\beta_{j}(t)\}_{j=1}^{\infty} is a family of independent Wiener processes defined on a filtered probability space (Ω,ℱ,ℱt,ℙ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{F}_{t},\mathbb{P}) satisfying the usual conditions. Without loss of generality, we can take

Ω:=𝒞0​(0,∞,H)\Omega:=\mathcal{C}_{0}(0,\infty;H)

to be the space of continuous function taking values in HH and vanishing at t=0t=0, and ℱ\mathcal{F} is the completion of the Borel σ\sigma-algebra associated with the local uniform convergence in this space. The operator (−∂x​x)s=D2​s(-\partial_{xx})^{s}=D^{2s} in 2.1 is the Fourier multiplier defined by

(D2​s​f)∧​(ξ)=|ξ|2​s​f^​(ξ),2​s≥0.(D^{2s}f)^{\wedge}(\xi)=\lvert\xi\rvert^{2s}\hat{f}(\xi),\quad 2s\geq 0.

When κ=0\kappa=0 and F⁡(u)=u2/2F(u)=u^{2}/2, equation 2.1 reduces to the classical Burgers equation with damping:

ut+a​u+u​ux−ν​ux​x=h+η.u_{t}+au+uu_{x}-\nu u_{xx}=h+\eta. (2.2)

We have the following assumptions. First, we assume that the growth and regularity of F′F^{\prime} is controlled by κ1\kappa_{1} as follows:

F′∈Lip1+κ1,κ1​{=0,κ=0,∈[0,κ),κ>0,F^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Lip}_{1+\kappa_{1}},\quad\kappa_{1}\begin{cases}=0,&\kappa=0,\\ \in[0,\kappa),&\kappa>0,\end{cases} (H1)

where

Lip1+s:={G​ locally Lipschitz:supx|G⁡(x)||x|1+s+supx≠y|G′​(x)−G′​(y)||x−y|s<∞},s≥0.\mathrm{Lip}_{1+s}:=\Bigl\{G\text{ locally Lipschitz}:\sup_{x}\frac{\lvert G(x)\rvert}{\lvert x\rvert^{1+s}}+\sup_{x\neq y}\frac{\lvert G^{\prime}(x)-G^{\prime}(y)\rvert}{\lvert x-y\rvert^{s}}<\infty\Bigr\},\quad s\geq 0.

Second, we assume that the noise is sufficiently regular and has mild decay at ∞\infty:

ej∈H1+κ,h∈H,φ1+κ1​(2+κ)h∈H,ℬ0:=∑j≥1|bj|2<∞,ℬ1:=∑j≥1|bj|2∥ej∥1+κ2<∞,ℬφ,m:=∑j=1∞|bj|2∥φmej∥2<∞,\begin{split}&e_{j}\in H^{1+\kappa},\quad h\in H,\quad\varphi^{1+\kappa_{1}(2+\kappa)}h\in H,\\ &\mathcal{B}_{0}:=\sum_{j\geq 1}\lvert b_{j}\rvert^{2}<\infty,\quad\mathcal{B}_{1}:=\sum_{j\geq 1}\lvert b_{j}\rvert^{2}\lVert e_{j}\rVert_{1+\kappa}^{2}<\infty,\quad\mathcal{B}_{\varphi,m}:=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\lvert b_{j}\rvert^{2}\lVert\varphi^{m}e_{j}\rVert^{2}<\infty,\end{split} (H2)

where φ⁡(x)=ln⁡(2+x2)\varphi(x)=\ln(2+x^{2}) and m≥1m\geq 1 satisfies an explicit lower bound 5.3 depending on κ1,κ\kappa_{1},\kappa; in particular, when κ1=0\kappa_{1}=0, m=1m=1 is sufficient. Lastly, when κ=0\kappa=0, we assume additionally that

{ej}j≥1​ is an unconditional basis for Hs0​(ℝ) for some s0∈(0,1/2).\{e_{j}\}_{j\geq 1}\text{ is an unconditional basis for~$H^{s_{0}}(\mathbb{R})$ for some~$s_{0}\in(0,1/2)$}. (H3)

We recall the following definition and result about unconditional basis used in this paper; see also [Hei11, Chap 7-8].

Definition 2.1

Let XX be a Banach space and {xn}⊂X\{x_{n}\}\subset X.

  1. 1.

    {xn}\{x_{n}\} is a Schauder basis for XX if for every x∈Xx\in X, there exist unique scalar an​(x)a_{n}(x) such that

    x=∑nan​(x)​xn.x=\sum_{n}a_{n}(x)x_{n}. (2.3)
  2. 2.

    {xn}\{x_{n}\} is called an unconditional basis if the series in 2.3 converges unconditionally.

Proposition 2.1

If {en}n=1∞\{e_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty} is an orthonormal basis of L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) and an unconditional basis for Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}), then there exist weights {wn}n=1∞\{w_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty} so that the map

U:Hs​(ℝ)→ℓ2​(w),U​f↦(⟨f,en⟩L2)n=1∞,U:H^{s}(\mathbb{R})\to\ell^{2}(w),\quad Uf\mapsto\bigl(\langle f,e_{n}\rangle_{L^{2}}\bigr)_{n=1}^{\infty},

is a Hilbert-space isomorphism, that is, for some c,C>0c,C>0,

c​∑n=1∞⟨f,en⟩2≤∥f∥Hs​(ℝ)2≤C​∑n=1∞⟨f,en⟩2.c\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\langle f,e_{n}\rangle^{2}\leq\lVert f\rVert^{2}_{H^{s}(\mathbb{R})}\leq C\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\langle f,e_{n}\rangle^{2}.

A canonical example for {en}n=1∞\{e_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty} satisfying H3 are sufficiently smooth wavelet functions; see [Mey92, Proposition 1, Chapter 6.4].

Based on the well-posedness theory of stochastic viscous conservation law equation 1.1 in Section 3.1, the white-forced viscous conservation law equation 1.1 defines a Markov family (ut,ℙu)(u_{t},\mathbb{P}_{u}) parameterized by the initial condition u∈Hu\in H. Let Pt​(u,A):=ℙ⁡(ut​(u,ω)∈A)P_{t}(u,A):=\mathbb{P}(u_{t}(u,\omega)\in A) be the transition function. We introduce the Markov operators ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t} and ℬt∗\mathcal{B}_{t}^{*} associated with PtP_{t}; see Section 3.2 for the detailed definitions.

If μ∈𝒫⁡(H)\mu\in\mathcal{P}(H) such that ℬt∗​μ=μ\mathcal{B}_{t}^{*}\mu=\mu for any t≥0t\geq 0, the measure μ\mu is called an invariant measure for the Markov family (ut,ℙu)(u_{t},\mathbb{P}_{u}). The invariant measure is a powerful tool for describing the long-term behavior of random dynamical systems.

The main result in this paper is the following.

Theorem 2.2

Let a,ν>0a,\nu>0 and κ≥0\kappa\geq 0. Assume H1, H2 and additionally H3 if κ=0\kappa=0. Then there exists an integer N≥1N\geq 1 such that as long as

bj≠0,1≤j≤N,b_{j}\neq 0,\quad 1\leq j\leq N,

and

h∈span⁡{e1,…,eN}h\in\mathrm{span}\{e_{1},\dotsc,e_{N}\} (2.4)

holds, the white-forced viscous conservation law equation 1.1 admits a unique invariant measure μ∈𝒫⁡(H)\mu\in\mathcal{P}(H) with polynomial mixing rate (1+t)−p(1+t)^{-p}, with p∈(1,q∗/2−1)p\in(1,q^{\ast}/2-1). Here, the constant q∗=q∗​(κ1,κ,m)∈(4,∞]q^{\ast}=q^{\ast}(\kappa_{1},\kappa,m)\in(4,\infty] is explicitly defined in 5.6, equals to ∞\infty when κ1=0\kappa_{1}=0, and grows linearly in mm for large mm when κ1>0\kappa_{1}>0. Moreover, for any p∈(1,q∗/2−1)p\in(1,q^{\ast}/2-1), there is a constant Cp>0C_{p}>0 such that

|𝔼​f​(u⁡(t))−∫Hf⁡(u)​μ​(𝑑u)|≤Cp​∥f∥Lip​(1+t)−p​(1+∥u0∥2),t≥0,\Big\lvert\mathbb{E}f\bigl(u(t)\bigr)-\int_{H}f(u)\,\mu(du)\Big\rvert\leq C_{p}\lVert f\rVert_{\mathrm{Lip}}(1+t)^{-p}\bigl(1+\lVert u_{0}\rVert^{2}\bigr),\quad t\geq 0, (2.5)

for any initial data u0∈Hu_{0}\in H and any bounded Lipschitz-continuous function f:H→ℝf:H\to\mathbb{R}.

Remark 2.1

The estimate 2.5 is equivalent to the following estimate

∥Pt(u0,⋅)−μ∥L⁡(H)∗≤Cp(1+∥u0∥2)(1+t)−p,t≥0,\begin{split}\|P_{t}(u_{0},\cdot)-\mu\|_{L(H)}^{*}\leq C_{p}(1+\|u_{0}\|^{2})(1+t)^{-p},~t\geq 0,\end{split}

and also to

∥ℬt∗λ−μ∥L⁡(H)∗≤Cp(1+∥u0∥2)(1+t)−p,t≥0,\begin{split}\|\mathcal{B}_{t}^{*}\lambda-\mu\|_{L(H)}^{*}\leq C_{p}(1+\|u_{0}\|^{2})(1+t)^{-p},~t\geq 0,\end{split}

for any λ∈𝒫⁡(H)\lambda\in\mathcal{P}(H).

Theorem 2.2 provides a polynomial mixing result for the white-forced classical viscous Burgers equation 2.2. For future reference, we state it explicitly as follows.

Corollary 2.3

Let a,ν>0a,\nu>0. Assume H1, H2 and H3. Then, there exists an integer N≥1N\geq 1 such that as long as

bj≠0,1≤j≤N,b_{j}\neq 0,\quad 1\leq j\leq N,

and 2.4 holds, the white-forced classical viscous Burgers equation 2.2 admits a unique invariant measure μ∈𝒫⁡(H){\mu\in\mathcal{P}(H)} with polynomial mixing rate (1+t)−p(1+t)^{-p}, for any p>1p>1. More precisely, for every p>1p>1, there exists a constant Cp>1C_{p}>1 such that

|𝔼f(u(t))−∫Hf(u)μ(du)|≤Cp∥f∥Lip(1+∥u0∥2)(1+t)−p,t≥0,u0∈H.\begin{split}\Big\lvert\mathbb{E}f\bigl(u(t)\bigr)-\int_{H}f(u)\,\mu(du)\Big\rvert\leq C_{p}\lVert f\rVert_{\mathrm{Lip}}\bigl(1+\lVert u_{0}\rVert^{2}\bigr)(1+t)^{-p},\quad t\geq 0,\quad u_{0}\in H.\end{split}

3 Coupling method

3.1 Well-posedness for 1.1

In this section we sketch the well-posedness theory of 1.1, based on the variational framework in [AV24]. The setting is simplified by the additive noise and polynomial nonlinearity.

Let V=V1=Hγ{V=V_{1}=H^{\gamma}} and V∗=V0=H−γ{V^{\ast}=V_{0}=H^{-\gamma}}, where γ=1+κ\gamma=1+\kappa, and Vθ=[V0,V1]θV_{\theta}=[V_{0},V_{1}]_{\theta} be the interpolation space. In particular, H=H∗=L2​(ℝ)=V1/2H=H^{\ast}=L^{2}(\mathbb{R})=V_{1/2}. We rewrite 1.1 as

d​u​(t)+A⁡(t,u⁡(t))​d​t=Q​d​Wt,du(t)+A\bigl(t,u(t)\bigr)\,dt=QdW_{t},

where WW is a cylindrical Wiener process on HH, and

Q:H→H;v↦∑j=1∞bj​⟨v,ej⟩​ejQ:H\to H;\quad v\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}b_{j}\langle v,e_{j}\rangle e_{j}

is a Hilbert–Schmidt operator due to the condition ∑j=1∞bj2<∞\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}b_{j}^{2}<\infty. The operator AA takes the forms

A(t,u)=A0u−ℱ(u)−h,A0u=ν(−∂x​x)γu+au,ℱ(u)=−(F(u))x,A(t,u)=A_{0}u-\mathcal{F}(u)-h,\quad A_{0}u=\nu(-\partial_{xx})^{\gamma}u+au,\quad\mathcal{F}(u)=-(F(u))_{x},

Theorem 3.1

Suppose AA satisfies

  1. 1.

    (coercivity) there exists θ>0\theta>0 such that

    ⟨A0​u,u⟩≥θ​∥u∥V2;\langle A_{0}u,u\rangle\geq\theta\lVert u\rVert^{2}_{V};
  2. 2.

    (boundedness of A0A_{0}) there exists C>0C>0 such that

    ∥A0​w∥V∗≤C​∥w∥V;\lVert A_{0}w\rVert_{V^{\ast}}\leq C\lVert w\rVert_{V};
  3. 3.

    (Lipschitzness and local monotonicity) there exist ρ≥0\rho\geq 0 and β∈(1/2,1)\beta\in(1/2,1) such that

    2​β≤1+1ρ+1,2\beta\leq 1+\frac{1}{\rho+1}, (3.1)

    so that

    ∥ℱ⁡(u)−ℱ⁡(v)∥V∗≲(1+∥u∥Vβρ+∥v∥Vβρ)​∥u−v∥Vβ.\lVert\mathcal{F}(u)-\mathcal{F}(v)\rVert_{V^{\ast}}\lesssim(1+\lVert u\rVert_{V_{\beta}}^{\rho}+\lVert v\rVert_{V_{\beta}}^{\rho})\lVert u-v\rVert_{V_{\beta}}. (3.2)

𝖯(σ<∞,supt∈[0,σ)∥u(t)∥H2+∫0σ∥u(t)∥V2dt<∞)=0.\mathsf{P}\bigl(\sigma<\infty,\ \sup_{t\in[0,\sigma)}\lVert u(t)\rVert^{2}_{H}+\int_{0}^{\sigma}\lVert u(t)\rVert_{V}^{2}\,dt<\infty\bigr)=0.

Under our setting, the blowup time is ∞\infty due to the a priori energy estimate that follows from Section 5.1. The first and second assumptions in Theorem 3.1 are routine to check. We will here verify the third assumption, that is, identity ρ\rho and β\beta in 3.1 and 3.2. Indeed,

∥ℱ⁡(u)−ℱ⁡(v)∥V∗\displaystyle\lVert\mathcal{F}(u)-\mathcal{F}(v)\rVert_{V^{\ast}} =sup∥w∥Hγ≤1⟨−∂xF(u)+∂xF(v),w⟩\displaystyle=\sup_{\lVert w\rVert_{H^{\gamma}}\leq 1}\langle-\partial_{x}F(u)+\partial_{x}F(v),w\rangle
=sup∥w∥Hγ≤1⟨F⁡(u)−F⁡(v),∂xw⟩\displaystyle=\sup_{\lVert w\rVert_{H^{\gamma}}\leq 1}\langle F(u)-F(v),\partial_{x}w\rangle

3.2 An abstract coupling criterion

In order to prove Theorem 2.2, we recall a general criterion from [Gao26], which gives sufficient conditions for polynomial mixing.

Let XX be a separable Banach space with a norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|. Let (ut,ℙu)(u_{t},\mathbb{P}_{u}) be a Feller family of Markov processes in XX, Pt​(u,A):=ℙ⁡(ut​(u,ω)∈A)P_{t}(u,A):=\mathbb{P}(u_{t}(u,\omega)\in A) is the transition function. We introduce the following associated Markov operators

ℬt:Cb(X)→Cb(X),ℬtf(u):=∫Xf(v)Pt(u,dv),∀f∈Cb(X),ℬt∗:𝒫(X)→𝒫(X),ℬt∗λ(A):=∫XPt(u,A)λ(du),∀λ∈𝒫(X).\begin{split}&\mathcal{B}_{t}:C_{b}(X)\rightarrow C_{b}(X),~\mathcal{B}_{t}f(u):=\int_{X}f(v)P_{t}(u,dv),~\forall f\in C_{b}(X),\\ &\mathcal{B}_{t}^{*}:\mathcal{P}(X)\rightarrow\mathcal{P}(X),~\mathcal{B}_{t}^{*}\lambda(A):=\int_{X}P_{t}(u,A)\lambda(du),~\forall\lambda\in\mathcal{P}(X).\end{split}
Definition 3.1

(See [Shi08, KS12]) Let (𝐮t,𝐏𝐮)(\mathbf{u}_{t},\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{u}}) be a Markov family in X×XX\times X, (𝐮t,𝐏𝐮)(\mathbf{u}_{t},\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{u}}) is called an extension of (ut,ℙu)(u_{t},\mathbb{P}_{u}) if for any 𝐮=(u,u′)∈X×X\mathbf{u}=(u,u^{\prime})\in X\times X the laws under 𝐏𝐮\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{u}} of processes {Π1​𝐮t}t≥0\{\Pi_{1}\mathbf{u}_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} and {Π2​𝐮t}t≥0\{\Pi_{2}\mathbf{u}_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} coincide with those of {ut}t≥0\{u_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} under ℙu\mathbb{P}_{u} and ℙu′\mathbb{P}_{u^{\prime}} respectively, where Π1\Pi_{1} and Π2\Pi_{2} denote the projections from X×XX\times X to the first and second component.

We are now in a position to present an abstract criterion for polynomial mixing, established in [Gao26]; see [Gao24] for a more readily applicable version. This criterion is the main tool we use to prove Theorem 2.2.

3.3 Construction of an extension

We outline how to construct an extension (𝐮t,𝐏𝐮)(\mathbf{u}_{t},\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{u}}), this is inspired by the works [KS12, NZ24a, Gao26].

Let {u⁡(t)}t≥0\{u(t)\}_{t\geq 0} and {u′​(t)}t≥0\{u^{\prime}(t)\}_{t\geq 0} be the solution to 1.1 with initial conditions u,u′∈Hu,u^{\prime}\in H. Let {v⁡(t)}t≥0\{v(t)\}_{t\geq 0} be the solution to the following auxillary process

{vt+F(v)x+av+𝖯N[F(u)x−F(v)x]=−ν(−∂x​x)1+κv+h+η.v|t=0=u′.\left\{\begin{aligned} &v_{t}+F(v)_{x}+av+\mathsf{P}_{N}\bigl[F(u)_{x}-F(v)_{x}\bigr]=-\nu(-\partial_{xx})^{1+\kappa}v+h+\eta.\\ &v\big|_{t=0}=u^{\prime}.\end{aligned}\right. (3.5)

  1. 1.

    𝐏~{𝔘′∈⋅}=ℙ{u′∈⋅}\tilde{\mathbf{P}}\{\mathfrak{U}^{\prime}\in\cdot\}={\mathbb{P}}\{u^{\prime}\in\cdot\}, 𝐏~(𝔙∈⋅)=ℙ(v∈⋅)\tilde{\mathbf{P}}(\mathfrak{V}\in\cdot)={\mathbb{P}}(v\in\cdot);

  2. 2.

    𝐏~{𝔘′≠𝔙}=∥ℒ({v(t)}[0,𝒯])−ℒ({u′(t)}[0,𝒯])∥T​V\tilde{\mathbf{P}}\{\mathfrak{U}^{\prime}\neq\mathfrak{V}\}=\lVert\mathcal{L}(\{v(t)\}_{[0,\mathcal{T}]})-\mathcal{L}(\{u^{\prime}(t)\}_{[0,\mathcal{T}]})\rVert_{TV};

Writing v~t=𝔙t​(ω,u,u′)\tilde{v}_{t}=\mathfrak{V}_{t}(\omega;u,u^{\prime}) and u~t′=𝔘t′​(ω,u,u′)\tilde{u}^{\prime}_{t}=\mathfrak{U}^{\prime}_{t}(\omega;u,u^{\prime}). Then the process {v~​(t)}t∈[0,𝒯]\{\tilde{v}(t)\}_{t\in[0,\mathcal{T}]} solves

{v~t+F(v~)x+av~+𝖯N(−F(v~)x)=−ν(−∂x​x)1+κv~+h+Λ,v~|t=0=u′,\left\{\begin{aligned} &\tilde{v}_{t}+F(\tilde{v})_{x}+a\tilde{v}+\mathsf{P}_{N}\bigl(-F(\tilde{v})_{x}\bigr)=-\nu(-\partial_{xx})^{1+\kappa}\tilde{v}+h+\Lambda,\\ &\tilde{v}\big|_{t=0}=u^{\prime},\end{aligned}\right.

where

{Λ⁡(t)}t∈[0,𝒯]=d{η⁡(t)−𝖯N​(F​(u)x)}t∈[0,𝒯].\{\Lambda(t)\}_{t\in[0,\mathcal{T}]}{\ \stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}\ }\bigl\{\eta(t)-\mathsf{P}_{N}\bigl(F(u)_{x}\bigr)\bigr\}_{t\in[0,\mathcal{T}]}.

Now let {u~​(t)}t∈[0,𝒯]\{\tilde{u}(t)\}_{t\in[0,\mathcal{T}]} solves

We now construct the mixing extension as follows. Let {(Ωk,ℱk,𝐏~k)}k≥0\bigl\{(\Omega^{k},\mathcal{F}^{k},\tilde{\mathbf{P}}^{k})\bigr\}_{k\geq 0} be independent copies of the space (Ω~,ℱ~,𝐏~)(\tilde{\Omega},\tilde{\mathcal{F}},\tilde{\mathbf{P}}), and let (Θ,𝒢,𝐏)(\Theta,\mathcal{G},\mathbf{P}) be their direct product. The random elements 𝔘,𝔘′\mathfrak{U},\mathfrak{U}^{\prime} can also be viewed as measurable maps defined on Ωk\Omega^{k}. For any u,u′∈Hu,u^{\prime}\in H and ω=(ω1,ω2,…)∈Θ\omega=(\omega^{1},\omega^{2},\dotsc)\in\Theta, let u~0=u\tilde{u}_{0}=u, u~0′=u′\tilde{u}^{\prime}_{0}=u^{\prime}, and recursively

u~t:=𝔘s​(ωk,u~k​𝒯​(ω),u~k​𝒯′​(ω)),u~t′:=𝔘s′​(ωk,u~k​𝒯​(ω),u~k​𝒯′​(ω)),t=s+k​𝒯,s∈[0,𝒯),k≥0,\tilde{u}_{t}:=\mathfrak{U}_{s}\bigl(\omega^{k};\tilde{u}_{k\mathcal{T}}(\omega),\tilde{u}^{\prime}_{k\mathcal{T}}(\omega)\bigr),\quad\tilde{u}^{\prime}_{t}:=\mathfrak{U}^{\prime}_{s}\bigl(\omega^{k};\tilde{u}_{k\mathcal{T}}(\omega),\tilde{u}^{\prime}_{k\mathcal{T}}(\omega)\bigr),\quad t=s+k\mathcal{T},\ s\in[0,\mathcal{T}),\ k\geq 0,

The goal is to show that for suitably chosen 𝒯\mathcal{T}, for 𝐮t:=(u~t,u~t′)\mathbf{u}_{t}:=(\tilde{u}_{t},\tilde{u}^{\prime}_{t}), the coupling (𝐮t,𝐏𝐮)(\mathbf{u}_{t},\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{u}}) is the desired mixing extension of (ut,ℙu)(u_{t},{\mathbb{P}}_{u}). The details will be given in Section 6. We briefly describe the mechanism below.

Due to the dissipation and damping, the Foiaş–Prodi estimate guaranteed that ∥u~​(t)−v~​(t)∥\lVert\tilde{u}(t)-\tilde{v}(t)\rVert (which has the same law as ∥u⁡(t)−v⁡(t)∥\lVert u(t)-v(t)\rVert under ℙ{\mathbb{P}}) decays exponentially, as long as certain energy of u~,u~′,v~\tilde{u},\tilde{u}^{\prime},\tilde{v} grow at most linearly. Thus, we introduce a stopping time σ=σ1∧τ~\sigma=\sigma_{1}\wedge\tilde{\tau}, where

σ1\displaystyle\sigma_{1} ≈ the first time ​u~′≠v~,\displaystyle\approx\text{ the first time }\tilde{u}^{\prime}\neq\tilde{v},
τ~\displaystyle\tilde{\tau} ≈ the first time energy of ​u~​(t),u~′​(t),v~​(t)​ reach ​C​(1+t).\displaystyle\approx\text{ the first time energy of }\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{u}^{\prime}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\text{ reach }C(1+t).

When t≤σ1t\leq\sigma_{1}, the Foiaş–Prodi estimate will help to control ∥u~​(t)−u~′​(t)∥\lVert\tilde{u}(t)-\tilde{u}^{\prime}(t)\rVert, this is the first condition in polynomial squeezing. Using a martingale inequality we can have power-law tail bound on τ~\tilde{\tau}, and by Girsanov transform we can estimate the total variational distance dT​V​(v~​(k​𝒯),u~′​(k​𝒯))d_{TV}(\tilde{v}(k\mathcal{T}),\tilde{u}^{\prime}(k\mathcal{T})), which leads to a power-law tail bound for σ1\sigma_{1}. Combining these we obtain the remaining condition.

4 Foiaş–Prodi estimate

4.1 Two Poincaré-type inequalities

The first Poincaré-type inequality also appears in [NZ24a, Lemma 3.1]. We present a brief proof here for completeness.

Lemma 4.1

Let A>0A>0. For every ε>0{\varepsilon}>0 and s>0s>0, there exists N=NεN=N_{{\varepsilon}} such that

∥𝖰N​χA​f∥≤ε​∥f∥Hs.\lVert\mathsf{Q}_{N}\chi_{A}f\rVert\leq{\varepsilon}\lVert f\rVert_{H^{s}}.

Proof: It suffices to show that TN:=𝖰N∘χA:Hs→L2T_{N}:=\mathsf{Q}_{N}\circ\chi_{A}:H^{s}\to L^{2} converges strongly to 00. The statement follows from the compactness of the operator χA:Hs→L2\chi_{A}:H^{s}\to L^{2} by Rellich–Kondrachov theory, and that 𝖰N:L2→L2\mathsf{Q}_{N}:L^{2}\to L^{2} converges strongly to 00 as N→∞N\to\infty. □\Box

The second Poincaré-type inequality concerns TN∗=χA∘𝖰NT^{\ast}_{N}=\chi_{A}\circ\mathsf{Q}_{N}, which is only applicable to unconditional basis. This will be key step in the proof of the Foiasş–Prodi estimate for 1.1.

Lemma 4.2

If {en}n=1∞\{e_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty} is an unconditional basis for Hs​(ℝ)​(s>0)H^{s}(\mathbb{R})(s>0), then there exists N=N⁡(ε)N=N({\varepsilon}) such that

∥χA​𝖰N​f∥≤ε​∥f∥Hs.\lVert\chi_{A}\mathsf{Q}_{N}f\rVert\leq{\varepsilon}\lVert f\rVert_{H^{s}}.

Proof: Let UU and ℓ2​(w)\ell^{2}(w) be introduced in Proposition 2.1. Then

‖f‖Hs2≍∑n=1∞wn​|⟨f,en⟩|2.\|f\|_{H^{s}}^{2}\asymp\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}w_{n}|\langle f,e_{n}\rangle|^{2}.

We can write TN∗=K​𝖰~N​UT^{\ast}_{N}=K\tilde{\mathsf{Q}}_{N}U, where K=χA∘U−1:ℓ2​(w)→L2​(ℝ)K=\chi_{A}\circ U^{-1}:\ell^{2}(w)\to L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) is a compact operator, and 𝖰~N=U​𝖰N​U−1:ℓ2​(w)→ℓ2​(w)\tilde{\mathsf{Q}}_{N}=U\mathsf{Q}_{N}U^{-1}:\ell^{2}(w)\to\ell^{2}(w) is the truncation to the post-NN coordinates. It suffices to show the strong convergence

limN→∞∥K​𝖰~N​f∥L2​(ℝ)→0,f∈ℓ2​(w).\lim_{N\to\infty}\lVert K\tilde{\mathsf{Q}}_{N}f\rVert_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}\to 0,\quad f\in\ell^{2}(w). (4.1)

Indeed, let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be the set of operators K:ℓ2​(w)→L2​(ℝ)K:\ell^{2}(w)\to L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) such that 4.1 holds. We will show that

  1. 1.

    The set 𝒮\mathcal{S} is norm closed, that is, if Km∈𝒮K_{m}\in\mathcal{S} and Km→KK_{m}\to K in operator norm, then K∈𝒮K\in\mathcal{S}.

  2. 2.

    If KK is finite-rank, then K∈𝒮K\in\mathcal{S}.

Then, since all compact operators between two Hilbert spaces can be approximated by finite-rank operators in the operator norm, 4.1 follows.

For the first item, the norm-closedness of 𝒮\mathcal{S} follows from

∥K​𝖰~N​f∥L2​(ℝ)≤∥K−Km∥ℓ2​(w)→L2​(ℝ)​∥f∥ℓ2​(w)+∥Km​𝖰~N​f∥ℓ2​(w)→L2​(ℝ).\lVert K\tilde{\mathsf{Q}}_{N}f\rVert_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}\leq\lVert K-K_{m}\rVert_{\ell^{2}(w)\to L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}\lVert f\rVert_{\ell^{2}(w)}+\lVert K_{m}\tilde{\mathsf{Q}}_{N}f\rVert_{\ell^{2}(w)\to L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}.

For the second item, writing c=(ci)∈ℓ2​(w)c=(c_{i})\in\ell^{2}(w), let KK be a finite-rank operator defined as

K⁡(c):=∑j=1Mϕj​(c)​yj,ϕj∈(ℓ2​(w))∗,yj∈L2​(ℝ).K(c):=\sum_{j=1}^{M}\phi_{j}(c)y_{j},\quad\phi_{j}\in(\ell^{2}(w))^{\ast},\ y_{j}\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}).

Then ϕj\phi_{j} can be identified as an element in ℓ2​(w−1)\ell^{2}(w^{-1}):

ϕj​(c)=∑k≥1aj(k)​ck,∑k=1∞|aj(k)|2/wj<∞.\phi_{j}(c)=\sum_{k\geq 1}a^{(k)}_{j}c_{k},\quad\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\lvert a^{(k)}_{j}\rvert^{2}/w_{j}<\infty.

Hence,

K​𝖰~N​(c)=∑j=1Myj​∑k≥Naj(k)​ck≤∑j=1M∥yj∥L2​∑k≥N|aj(k)|2/wk→0.K\tilde{\mathsf{Q}}_{N}(c)=\sum_{j=1}^{M}y_{j}\sum_{k\geq N}a^{(k)}_{j}c_{k}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{M}\lVert y_{j}\rVert_{L^{2}}\sum_{k\geq N}\lvert a^{(k)}_{j}\rvert^{2}/w_{k}\to 0.

This completes the proof. □\Box

Inspired by [Abe89, NZ24a], let us introduce a smooth space-time weight function. Let φ⁡(x)=ln⁡(2+x2)\varphi(x)=\ln(2+x^{2}) and

ut+au+ν(−∂x​x)1+κu+(F(u))x=h+η,vt+av+ν(−∂x​x)1+κv+𝖯N[F(u)x−F(v)x]+(F(v))x=h+η.\begin{split}&u_{t}+au+\nu(-\partial_{xx})^{1+\kappa}u+\bigl(F(u)\bigr)_{x}=h+\eta,\\ &v_{t}+av+\nu(-\partial_{xx})^{1+\kappa}v+\mathsf{P}_{N}\bigl[F(u)_{x}-F(v)_{x}\bigr]+\bigl(F(v)\bigr)_{x}=h+\eta.\end{split}

wt+aw+QN[F(u)x−F(v)x]=−ν(−∂x​x)1+κw.w_{t}+aw+Q_{N}\bigl[F(u)_{x}-F(v)_{x}\bigr]=-\nu(-\partial_{xx})^{1+\kappa}w. (4.3)

We define

ezα​(r):=∥z⁡(r)∥2​α​∥z⁡(r)∥1+κ2,e~z​(r):=∥ψ⁡(r)​z​(r)∥2​κ1​∥ψ⁡(r)​z​(r)∥1+κ2​for​r≥0.e_{z}^{\alpha}(r):=\lVert z(r)\rVert^{2\alpha}\lVert z(r)\rVert_{1+\kappa}^{2},\quad\tilde{e}_{z}(r):=\lVert\psi(r)z(r)\rVert^{2\kappa_{1}}\lVert\psi(r)z(r)\rVert_{1+\kappa}^{2}~~~{\rm{for}}~r\geq 0.

Now, we are in a position to state the Foiaş–Prodi estimate, for which Lemma 4.2 plays an important role in the proof.

Motivated by the works [KS12, NZ24a, Gao26], we introduce the following stopping times. For K≥1K\geq 1, we define

5.4 Estimate for auxiliary process

The goal of this section is to give a growth estimate of vv. The idea is to use the available estimate on u′u^{\prime} and use Girsanov theorem to control the effect of the finite dimension term

𝖯N​[F​(u)x−F​(v)x].\mathsf{P}_{N}[F(u)_{x}-F(v)_{x}]. (5.25)

To view 5.25 as a drift term of the noise and apply Girsanov, we need suitable truncation for the Novikov condition to hold. This motivates the definition of the truncated processes. Here we borrow some ideas from the works [NZ24a, Gao26, NZ24b, Gao24].

To be more precise, let

τ=τv∧τu∧τu′.\tau=\tau^{v}\wedge\tau^{u}\wedge\tau^{u^{\prime}}.

We define u^\hat{u} to be the truncated process of uu, such that u^​(t)=u​(t)\hat{u}(t)=u(t) when t≤τt\leq\tau, and u^\hat{u} solves the linear equation u^t+au^=−(−∂x​x)1+κu^\hat{u}_{t}+a\hat{u}=-(-\partial_{xx})^{1+\kappa}\hat{u} for t≥τt\geq\tau; the truncated processes u^′\hat{u}^{\prime} and v^\hat{v} are defined similarly. We can establish estimate for τu^\tau^{\hat{u}} and τu^′\tau^{\hat{u}^{\prime}} similar to Lemma 5.8. We recall that in Proposition 5.9 and in the remaining of this section, the constant p¯=p¯​(κ1,κ)\bar{p}=\bar{p}(\kappa_{1},\kappa) is introduced in 5.7.

Step 2. Let uu be the solution to 1.1 and u^\hat{u} be the truncated process defined as in above with an arbitrary stopping time τ\tau. Using 5.27-5.29, we can compare the energy between the original process and the truncated process. More precisely, for t≥0t\geq 0:

We consider the transform on Ω=𝒞0​(0,∞,H)\Omega=\mathcal{C}_{0}(0,\infty;H) defined by

(Φu,u′ω)t=ωt−∫0t𝕀{s≤τ}𝖯N(F(u)x−F(v)x)ds(\Phi^{u,u^{\prime}}\omega)_{t}=\omega_{t}-\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{I}_{\{s\leq\tau\}}\mathsf{P}_{N}\bigl(F(u)_{x}-F(v)_{x}\bigr)\,ds

Employing the strategy in [KS12, Section 3.3.3], we can estimate the total variation distance between ℙ{\mathbb{P}} and Φ∗u,u′​ℙ\Phi^{u,u^{\prime}}_{\ast}{\mathbb{P}}. In this section we will write

d=∥u−u′∥,R=∥u∥∨∥u′∥.d=\lVert u-u^{\prime}\rVert,R=\lVert u\rVert\vee\lVert u^{\prime}\rVert.
Proposition 5.10

Let τ\tau be defined for sufficiently large KK and ρ≥2\rho\geq 2. Let ϵ>0\epsilon>0. There exists N≥1N\geq 1 such that if bj≠0b_{j}\neq 0 for 1≤j≤N1\leq j\leq N, then for some constant CC depending on N,K,ϵN,K,\epsilon and max1≤j≤N⁡bj−1\max_{1\leq j\leq N}b_{j}^{-1}, such that

Ω=𝒞⁡(0,∞,𝖯N​H)⊕𝒞⁡(0,∞,𝖰N​H):=Ω(1)⊕Ω(2),\Omega=\mathcal{C}(0,\infty;\mathsf{P}_{N}H)\oplus\mathcal{C}(0,\infty;\mathsf{Q}_{N}H):=\Omega^{(1)}\oplus\Omega^{(2)},

Φu,u′​(ω(1),ω(2))=(Ψu,u′​(ω(1),ω(2)),ω(2)),ω=(ω(1),ω(2))∈Ω,\Phi^{u,u^{\prime}}(\omega^{(1)},\omega^{(2)})=\bigl(\Psi^{u,u^{\prime}}(\omega^{(1)},\omega^{(2)}),\omega^{(2)}\bigr),\quad\omega=(\omega^{(1)},\omega^{(2)})\in\Omega,

where Ψu,u′:Ω(1)→Ω(1)\Psi^{u,u^{\prime}}:\Omega^{(1)}\to\Omega^{(1)} is given by

The transform Ψu,u′\Psi^{u,u^{\prime}} is acting on a finite dimensional Wiener process, and hence by the Girsanov theorem, for each ω(2)\omega^{(2)}, we have

∥Ψ∗u,u′​(ℙN,ω(2))−ℙN∥T​V≤12​[(𝔼N​exp⁡(6​sup1≤j≤Nbj−2​∫0∞∥𝒜⁡(t,⋅,ω(2))∥2​𝑑t))1/2−1]1/2,\lVert\Psi^{u,u^{\prime}}_{\ast}({\mathbb{P}}_{N},\omega^{(2)})-{\mathbb{P}}_{N}\rVert_{TV}\leq\frac{1}{2}\Bigl[\Bigl(\mathbb{E}_{N}\exp\bigl(6\sup_{1\leq j\leq N}b_{j}^{-2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\lVert\mathcal{A}(t;\cdot,\omega^{(2)})\rVert^{2}\,dt\bigr)\Bigr)^{1/2}-1\Bigr]^{1/2}, (5.31)

is satisfied for some c>0c>0.

6 Proof of Main result

The goal of this section is to prove Theorem 2.2, by constructing a extension and show that it satisfies the properties 3.3 and 3.4 in Theorem 2.2. The outline is as follows.

  1. 1.

    Pick 𝒯>0\mathcal{T}>0, and construct a extension as outlined in Section 3.3.

  2. 2.

    Show that for any ball B=BH​(0,d)B=B_{H}(0,d), τ𝐁\tau_{\mathbf{B}} has exponential moments. This is done by Proposition 6.4, which actually specifies the choice of 𝒯\mathcal{T}. This verifies 3.3, with g⁡(r)=1+r2g(r)=1+r^{2}.

  3. 3.

    Build the stopping time σ\sigma needed for 3.4 out of stopping times τu,τu′\tau^{u},\tau^{u^{\prime}} introduced in Sections 5.4 and 5.3. This requires choices of the constants K,ρK,\rho. In Section 6.2 we will show that if KK and ρ\rho chosen sufficiently large and δ\delta is sufficiently small, then the resulting stopping time will satisfy 3.4 with B=BH​(0,δ)B=B_{H}(0,\delta).

The resulting extension then satisfies the assumptions of Theorem 2.2, and Theorem 2.2 follows immediately from Theorem 3.2.

𝐏𝐮(σ=∞)≥1−∑k=0∞𝐏𝐮{σ∈[k𝒯,(k+1)𝒯]}≥1−12∑k=0∞1(1+k)q/2≥1−π212>0.\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{u}}(\sigma=\infty)\geq 1-\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{u}}\Bigl\{\sigma\in[k\mathcal{T},(k+1)\mathcal{T}]\Bigr\}\geq 1-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(1+k)^{q/2}}\geq 1-\frac{\pi^{2}}{12}>0.

This is the second inequality in 3.4. The third inequality follows from

𝐄𝐮(𝕀{σ<∞}σp0)≤∑k=0∞𝐄𝐮(𝕀{σ∈[k𝒯,(k+1)𝒯]}σp0)≲∑k=0∞q,𝒯⁡(k+1)p0⋅12​(1+k)q/2≲∑k=0∞q,𝒯⁡1(k+1)q/2−p0<∞.\begin{split}\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{u}}(\mathbb{I}_{\{\sigma<\infty\}}\sigma^{p_{0}})&\leq\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\Bigl(\mathbb{I}_{\{\sigma\in[k\mathcal{T},(k+1)\mathcal{T}]\}}\sigma^{p_{0}}\Bigr)\\ &\lesssim_{q,\mathcal{T}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+1)^{p_{0}}\cdot\frac{1}{2(1+k)^{q/2}}\lesssim_{q,\mathcal{T}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(k+1)^{q/2-p_{0}}}<\infty.\end{split}

The fourth inequality follows from

𝐄𝐮(𝕀{σ<∞}(∥u~(σ)∥2​p0+∥u~′(σ)∥2​p0))≤Cp0(∥u~(0)∥2​p0+∥u~′(0)∥2​p0+𝐄𝐮(𝕀{σ<∞}(1+σp0)))≤Cp0.\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\Bigl(\mathbb{I}_{\{\sigma<\infty\}}\bigl(\lVert\tilde{u}(\sigma)\rVert^{2p_{0}}+\lVert\tilde{u}^{\prime}(\sigma)\rVert^{2p_{0}}\bigr)\Bigr)\leq C_{p_{0}}\bigl(\lVert\tilde{u}(0)\rVert^{2p_{0}}+\lVert\tilde{u}^{\prime}(0)\rVert^{2p_{0}}+\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\bigl(\mathbb{I}_{\{\sigma<\infty\}}(1+\sigma^{p_{0}})\bigr)\bigr)\leq C_{p_{0}}.

This finishes the proof. □\Box

For κ>0\kappa>0,

∥D1+κ​(f​g)−f​D1+κ​g∥L2≲∥∂xf∥L∞​∥Dκ​g∥L2+∥D1+κ​f∥L∞​∥g∥L2.\lVert D^{1+\kappa}(fg)-fD^{1+\kappa}g\rVert_{L^{2}}\lesssim\lVert\partial_{x}f\rVert_{L^{\infty}}\lVert D^{\kappa}g\rVert_{L^{2}}+\lVert D^{1+\kappa}f\rVert_{L^{\infty}}\lVert g\rVert_{L^{2}}. (A.1)

∥D1+κ​(f​g)−f​D1+κ​g−∂xf​D~κ​g−g​D1+κ​f∥L2≲∥D​f∥B​M​O​∥Dκ​g∥L2,\lVert D^{1+\kappa}(fg)-fD^{1+\kappa}g-\partial_{x}f\tilde{D}^{\kappa}g-gD^{1+\kappa}f\rVert_{L^{2}}\lesssim\lVert Df\rVert_{BMO}\lVert D^{\kappa}g\rVert_{L^{2}},

A.3 Martingale inequalities

We recall some martingale inequalities.

Lemma A.8

Let XtX_{t} be a non-negative super-martingale, then for every x>0x>0,

ℙ⁡(supt≥0Xt≥x)≤𝖤​X0x.{\mathbb{P}}(\sup_{t\geq 0}X_{t}\geq x)\leq\frac{\mathsf{E}X_{0}}{x}.

In particular, if MtM_{t} is a local martingale, then

ℙ⁡(supt≥0(Mt−γ​⟨M⟩t)≥ρ)=ℙ⁡(supt≥0eγ​Mt−γ22​⟨M⟩t≥eγ​ρ)≤e−γ​ρ.{\mathbb{P}}(\sup_{t\geq 0}(M_{t}-\gamma\langle M\rangle_{t})\geq\rho)={\mathbb{P}}(\sup_{t\geq 0}e^{\gamma M_{t}-\frac{\gamma^{2}}{2}\langle M\rangle_{t}}\geq e^{\gamma\rho})\leq e^{-\gamma\rho}.
Lemma A.9

Let MtM_{t} be a continuous martingale with M0=0M_{0}=0. Assume that for some q>0q>0,

𝔼​⟨M⟩tq/2≤Kq​tq/2,t≥1.\mathbb{E}\langle M\rangle_{t}^{q/2}\leq K_{q}t^{q/2},\quad t\geq 1. (A.5)

Then for every γ>0\gamma>0, there exists a constant C=Cq,γC=C_{q,\gamma} such that

ℙ⁡(supt≥0(Mt−γ​t)≥ρ)≤Cq,γ​Kq​ρ−q2,ρ≥2.{\mathbb{P}}\bigl(\sup_{t\geq 0}(M_{t}-\gamma t)\geq\rho\bigr)\leq C_{q,\gamma}K_{q}\rho^{-\frac{q}{2}},\quad\rho\geq 2.

Proof: Let k0∈ℕk_{0}\in\mathbb{N} be such that 2k0≤ρ<2k0+12^{k_{0}}\leq\rho<2^{k_{0}+1}. We have

ℙ⁡(supt≥0(Mt−γ​t)≥ρ)≤ℙ⁡(sup0≤t≤2k0(Mt−γ​t)≥ρ)+∑k=k0∞ℙ⁡(supt∈[2k,2k+1](Mt−γ​t)≥ρ)=:p1+p2.{\mathbb{P}}\bigl(\sup_{t\geq 0}(M_{t}-\gamma t)\geq\rho\bigr)\leq{\mathbb{P}}(\sup_{0\leq t\leq 2^{k_{0}}}(M_{t}-\gamma t)\geq\rho)+\sum_{k=k_{0}}^{\infty}{\mathbb{P}}\bigl(\sup_{t\in[2^{k},2^{k+1}]}(M_{t}-\gamma t)\geq\rho\bigr)=:p_{1}+p_{2}.

By Doob’s maximal inequality, Burkholder–Davis–Gundy inequality and A.5, we have

p1≤ℙ(sup0≤t≤2k0Mt≥ρ)≤𝔼​M2k0qρq≤Kq​2k0​q/2ρq≤Kqρ−q/2.p_{1}\leq{\mathbb{P}}\bigl(\sup_{0\leq t\leq 2^{k_{0}}}M_{t}\geq\rho\bigr)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}M_{2^{k_{0}}}^{q}}{\rho^{q}}\leq\frac{K_{q}2^{k_{0}q/2}}{\rho^{q}}\leq K_{q}\rho^{-q/2}. (A.6)

For p2p_{2}, similar to A.6 we have

ℙ⁡(supt∈[2k,2k+1](Mt−γ​t)≥ρ)≤ℙ⁡(supt∈[2k,2k+1]Mt≥ρ+γ​2k)≤ℙ⁡(supt∈[0,2k+1]Mt≥γ​2k)≤Kq​2(k+1)​q/2(γ​2k)q,{\mathbb{P}}\bigl(\sup_{t\in[2^{k},2^{k+1}]}(M_{t}-\gamma t)\geq\rho\bigr)\leq{\mathbb{P}}\bigl(\sup_{t\in[2^{k},2^{k+1}]}M_{t}\geq\rho+\gamma 2^{k}\bigr)\leq{\mathbb{P}}\bigl(\sup_{t\in[0,2^{k+1}]}M_{t}\geq\gamma 2^{k}\bigr)\leq K_{q}\frac{2^{(k+1)q/2}}{(\gamma 2^{k})^{q}},

and hence

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
